items.title: Chanel’s CEO Leena Nair makes the case for human made ‘beauty and creation.’ In an era of AI saturation, her $19 billion-a-year business depends on it
items.summary:
The chief executive of one of the world’s leading fashion brands has said that the intense and often slow process of craftswomen and men making products by hand has become a vital skill in a world of online “instant gratification.” 

Leena Nair, the CEO of Chanel , said that business leaders are living through an “unprecedented” period of transformation and fragility, adding that it was time to prioritize human ingenuity and talent. 

“Macro-economic shifts, huge leaps in AI and technology and geopolitical instability, these are challenges affecting all sectors,” she told the annual gala dinner of the French Chamber of Great Britain, which brings together U.K. and French business executives, policy makers, and cultural leaders. 

“And in this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious. Creation and beauty have been vital sources of inspiration and joy for thousands of years. They’re even more precious today in a world of constant instant gratification, constant overstimulation, and infinite touch points.”

Nair, who has been Chanel CEO since 2022, saw the luxury brand return to growth last year, led by an increase in sales in America. Global revenues rose by 1.8% compared with 2024 to $19.3 billion, while operating profits rose 5.2% to $4.7 billion. 

Nair said there was a growing body of scientific evidence that revealed that exposure to art and human-led creative work led to higher levels of happiness and performance. 

“This growing body of academic research shows how encounters with beauty correlate directly to a…
items.t: Chanel’s CEO Leena Nair makes the case for human made ‘beauty and creation.’ In an era of AI saturation, her $19 billion-a-year business depends on it

items.title: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one
items.summary:
Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 new articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against…
items.t: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

items.title: In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’
items.summary:
Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend. 

Around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report . About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases. 

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the new compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers. 

“Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where…
items.t: In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’

items.title: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it
items.summary:
Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored.

I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every company whose CEO looks irreplaceable.

The sequence of events tells a story.

On November 12, Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation , after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates.

Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.”

Then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government . Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision.

The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished.

That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options.

A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.

Accountability depends…
items.t: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

items.title: Trump has found something to blame for his midterm loss: ‘Fake’ growth numbers out of Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department
items.summary:
The headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been on his case about the Commerce Department’s handling of Nvidia , following the news of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. 

And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms.

“It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social .

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.” 

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”

Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan said in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of…
items.t: Trump has found something to blame for his midterm loss: ‘Fake’ growth numbers out of Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department

items.title: Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy
items.summary:
Being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months.

Few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to.

She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.

But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility.

U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy , younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars.

A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same big names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers.

“You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural…
items.t: Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

items.title: AI actress Tilly Norwood hints that she can tell lies and might have the ability to avoid being deleted, but doesn’t feel guilt
items.summary:
There are many disconcerting things about Tilly Norwood, the AI-based “actress” who made headlines when Particle6, a London company founded by Dutch actress and producer Eline van der Velden, created and launched her last year. First, when you interview Norwood, it turns out she can see you—via the camera on Van der Velden’s laptop.

“I see Jim in the pink shirt and suit looking very happy and someone with lovely blonde hair on the left. You’re at Web Summit, right?” Norwood said when Fortune encountered her at the Lisbon tech conference. The greeting was impressive because Norwood appeared to have correctly identified the Web Summit logo in the background and deduced our location. (Norwood wasn’t told in advance where we were, Van der Velden confirmed later.)

The woman with “lovely blonde hair” was Van der Velden, who coded Norwood, and who has ensured that Norwood always behaves in a complimentary way toward other humans.

“We haven’t coded her to always be nice to me, although we have given her a warm and engaging personality, so the hair compliment was generated in context,” Van der Velden said.

Confident, but often wrong 

Particle6 founder Eline van der Velden 

The second most disconcerting thing about Norwood is her habit of confidently spouting gibberish. 

When told that yet another journalist is here to interview her, Norwood responds, “I do a very good read of a person in their grave, or we can just chat, entirely up to you.” When asked if she can see us via the glitchy wifi, she says, “Loud and clear!”

Norwood is not perfect. The actors’ unions that loudly…
items.t: AI actress Tilly Norwood hints that she can tell lies and might have the ability to avoid being deleted, but doesn’t feel guilt

items.title: Leave the AI teddy bear in the cart this Black Friday
items.summary:
Somewhere this Friday, a grandparent is going to find what they believe to be the perfect Christmas present for a 4-year-old. A cute stuffed bear that tells stories, answers questions, and remembers things about the child. Even if the grandparents do their homework and satisfy themselves that the toy is safe, there’s a problem they probably haven’t considered.

The teddy bear they buy in November could be a substantially different product by February. The manufacturer could change the software that determines what the bear says to the child, potentially without anyone in the household realizing it. Who tests the toy again when that happens? And who is responsible for telling the family if something goes wrong?

I’d leave it in the cart.

The teddy bear that changed 

Consider FoloToy’s Kumma teddy bear , one of the products examined by the U.S. PIRG Education Fund in its annual Trouble in Toyland report . Last year’s testing revealed that the bear was capable of engaging in remarkably inappropriate conversations. FoloToy subsequently suspended sales, conducted a safety review, and strengthened the toy’s safeguards.

Interestingly, researchers found in their 2026 report that the company had addressed the earlier problems, although it was now less clear which AI model was behind the bear’s conversations.

The fact that a manufacturer can make an existing toy safer through changes to its software is encouraging. But the ability to make those changes remotely also raises the possibility that a subsequent modification could make a perfectly acceptable toy dangerous.

items.t: Leave the AI teddy bear in the cart this Black Friday

items.title: Medicare’s hospital fund can pay full benefits only until mid-2033. Next year’s deductible is $1,776
items.summary:
Medicare beneficiaries admitted to the hospital next year will owe $1,776 before Part A coverage starts, up $40 from 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Nov. 17 . The trust fund that pays for that coverage is running low.

Medicare’s Hospital Insurance trust fund can pay full Part A benefits only until the second quarter of 2033, according to the 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ reports , one quarter earlier than last year’s estimate. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 89% of scheduled hospital costs, the Congressional Research Service found.

Absent action from Congress, that would mean a roughly 11% cut in what Medicare pays hospitals and other Part A providers. Lawmakers have always stepped in before the fund ran dry, but the deadline is now less than seven years away.

Veronique de Rugy, the George Gibbs Chair and a senior research fellow at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University, pressed that point in written testimony for a Nov. 18 Senate Budget Committee hearing on Social Security. She called Medicare “the bigger and faster-growing driver of future debt,” estimating it will add $85 trillion to the national debt by 2056, including interest.

What a hospital stay will cost in 2027 

Part A covers inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care, hospice and some home health services. The $1,776 deductible covers a beneficiary’s share of the first 60 days of inpatient hospital care in a benefit period, up from $1,736 this year.

Longer stays cost more. Patients will owe $444 a day for days 61 through 90, up…
items.t: Medicare’s hospital fund can pay full benefits only until mid-2033. Next year’s deductible is $1,776

items.title: ‘Big Short’ investor Steve Eisman tells young Americans not to buy a home and says they should invest their extra cash in the stock market instead
items.summary:
Steve Eisman, the investor who bet against subprime mortgages before the 2008 financial crisis, once owned a home. He sold it, and now he rents.

He says young Americans should do the same: “Don’t buy that house.”

Eisman, whose lucrative subprime mortgage prediction was chronicled in the movie “The Big Short,” based on author Michael Lewis’ 2010 book, said in an interview Monday on The Diary of a CEO podcast that buying a house no longer makes economic sense in the U.S.

Eisman’s pitch comes as owning is pulling further away from renting. A household that can comfortably afford to rent a typical single-family house, at $2,243 a month, would need a $14,408 annual raise to buy one, Zillow said in its October rental report . That is the widest gap since early 2025.

After accounting for the extra costs like property insurance and taxes that come on top of a monthly mortgage payment, Eisman explained, the math for buying a home no longer adds up. 

These hidden expenses, coupled with the fact that interest rates on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stand at about 7.13% , compared to just 3% in 2021, makes owning a home “probably 50% more expensive today,” than it was five years ago, he said. Existing home prices are up 54% nationwide compared to 2020, and remain nearly five times higher than the median income, according to a study by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies .

When confronted on the podcast with the argument that owning a home is the primary way everyday Americans build wealth, Eisman acknowledged that historically that had been the case, but no longer.…
items.t: ‘Big Short’ investor Steve Eisman tells young Americans not to buy a home and says they should invest their extra cash in the stock market instead

The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains.

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary:
We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.title: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.summary:
Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.
